Digital Forensics Lab 3: Timeline Analysis, Incident Reconstruction & Forensic Reporting

Course: CYBR 2800
Lab: 3 of 3 — the capstone
Case Number: CYBR-2026-0042
Estimated Time: 5–7 hours
Total Points: 100
Difficulty: Intermediate / Advanced

Case Briefing

FROM: Office of General Counsel
TO: Digital Forensics Unit
RE: Case CYBR-2026-0042 — priority escalation
DATE: 2026-08-24

On 2026-08-21 our banking partner contacted Finance to ask why a reconciliation report containing live client account data had been seen outside our environment. Finance could not answer. The DLP team then pulled the endpoint alert queue and found fourteen unreviewed alerts going back to June, all from the same workstation.

That workstation is the one your unit already has open under the backup-server matter. It was powered down and imaged on 2026-08-24.

We need to know what left this company, how much of it, when, by what route, and whether the evidence supports a referral. Assume this report will be read by opposing counsel.

Previously, in Labs 1 and 2

This is not a new investigation. It is the third evidence source in the same case, and your earlier findings still apply.

What Lab 1 established

  • A workstation at 10.10.20.10 used by an employee named Alex was imaged and verified.
  • Deleted files existed in home/alex/Downloads/, and some were recoverable.
  • A script named maintenance.sh reached out to an internal server.

What Lab 2 added

  • A second device: backupadmin's external backup drive for backup01 (10.10.20.25), containing roughly 200 days of job logs.
  • A backup job on 2026-08-19 that failed with an authentication error.
  • A backup job on 2026-08-20 that ran outside the maintenance window using backupadmin's credentials.
  • Recovered temporary credentials for backupadmin that were never rotated.

What Lab 2 could not resolve

The open question: repeated SSH authentication failures arrived from 10.10.20.55 on the morning of 2026-08-20. Nothing in the Lab 2 evidence identified that host. It was not a server you had seen, and you had no basis to attribute it to a person.

At the end of Lab 2 the correct answer to “was this malicious?” was “not determinable from this evidence alone.” That was the right call then.

This lab is where that changes. The evidence to attribute 10.10.20.55 exists in the image you are about to examine. Nobody is going to tell you which file it is in.

What Is Different About This Evidence

The Lab 3 image is a full acquisition of Alex's workstation, not a slice of it. Compared to Lab 2 it is roughly twice the size and contains several categories of artifact you have not worked with yet:

  • Financial records. Real spreadsheet files with tens of thousands of transaction rows, bank account data, and dollar values. Some of them are deleted.
  • Application API logs. Thousands of individual HTTP requests against an internal finance reporting service, showing exactly which endpoints were called, by whom, how often, and how many bytes came back.
  • Messaging application history. Exported conversations from more than one chat client.
  • Infrastructure logs. DHCP, VPN, DLP, auditd, USB, and file-share access records.
  • Binary artifacts. Compressed spreadsheets and a packed archive. grep will not help you with these, and learning why is part of the lab.

The Lab 2 backup drive is reproduced inside this image at mnt/recovered_backup/ so you can re-examine your earlier findings against the new material.

Scale warning: the file listing runs to several hundred entries and the largest log has thousands of lines. Do not attempt to read these files top to bottom. Every part of this lab is designed around grep, cut, sort, uniq -c, and wc -l. If you find yourself scrolling, stop and write a filter instead.

Learning Objectives

By completing this lab, you should be able to:

  1. Create a forensic timeline from filesystem metadata.
  2. Explain which timestamps can be forged and which cannot.
  3. Recover deleted text, structured, and binary files from inode metadata.
  4. Extract and interpret evidence from a compressed file format.
  5. Quantify the scope of a data exposure from recovered records.
  6. Analyze application access logs to distinguish normal use from abuse.
  7. Analyze messaging-application artifacts.
  8. Attribute network activity to a device using correlated evidence.
  9. Identify anti-forensic behavior and explain what it does and does not prove.
  10. Eliminate alternative explanations rather than confirming a favored one.
  11. Reconstruct an incident from multiple independent sources.
  12. Distinguish confirmed facts from inference and from speculation.
  13. Produce a professional forensic report suitable for legal review.

Important Lab Rules

Authorized Evidence Only: Use only the instructor-provided forensic evidence image.

Do not investigate your personal computer, another student's computer, or any system for which you do not have authorization.

All analysis must be performed on a working copy. Never mount the original evidence image. Never mount either copy read-write.

The financial data in this image is synthetic. Every account number, client name, and dollar figure was generated for this exercise. None of it refers to a real person or institution. Handle it as though it were real anyway — that habit is the point.

Required Environment and Tools

You will need your Ubuntu forensic-analysis VM with:

Tools used in this lab
Tool Purpose New in Lab 3?
sha256sum Verify evidence integrity No
mmls Find the partition offset No
fsstat, fls, istat, icat Filesystem and inode examination No
tsk_recover Bulk file recovery No
mactime Render a bodyfile as a timeline Yes
file Identify a recovered file by content, not extension Yes
unzip, tar Open recovered compressed evidence Yes
blkls, foremost Carve unallocated space (fallback method) Yes
python3 Parse recovered spreadsheet data Yes

Install anything you are missing:

sudo apt update
sudo apt install sleuthkit foremost unzip python3 bc

libreoffice is optional. Everything required can be done with the command-line tools above.

Part 1 — Open the Case File

Create your Lab 3 working directory:

mkdir -p ~/CYBR2800_Lab3/{evidence,working,timeline,output,recovered,findings,screenshots,notes,report,hashes}
cd ~/CYBR2800_Lab3

Your structure should look like this:

CYBR2800_Lab3/
├── evidence/      original image, never touched
├── working/       the copy you analyze
├── timeline/      bodyfile and mactime output
├── output/        raw command output
├── recovered/     files pulled back from inodes
├── findings/      extracted financial data, parsed results
├── screenshots/
├── notes/
├── report/
└── hashes/

Start your investigation log now, not at the end:

nano notes/investigation_notes.md

Field note: record the inode number of every artifact you touch, as you touch it. You will be asked to produce them, and re-deriving an inode three hours later after you have run forty commands is miserable.

Part 2 — Verify the Evidence and Make a Working Copy

Copy the instructor-provided image into evidence/:

cp /path/to/CYBR2800_Lab3_Evidence.dd evidence/

Hash it and record the result:

sha256sum evidence/CYBR2800_Lab3_Evidence.dd | tee hashes/original_hash.txt

Compare that value against the SHA-256 published by your instructor.

If the hash does not match, stop. Check the file size first — a truncated download is the usual cause. If the size is correct and the hash still differs, notify your instructor and request a fresh copy. Do not analyze an image you cannot account for.

Create the working copy and prove it started identical:

cp evidence/CYBR2800_Lab3_Evidence.dd working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd
sha256sum working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd | tee hashes/working_hash.txt

Protect the original from yourself:

chmod 444 evidence/CYBR2800_Lab3_Evidence.dd

Document in your report

  • The published hash, your calculated hash, and whether they match.
  • The working-copy hash and the time you created it.
  • Why hashing the working copy matters to chain of custody.

Part 3 — Map the Disk

Describe the image:

img_stat working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd | tee output/img_stat.txt

Find the partition table:

mmls working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd | tee output/mmls.txt

This is the step everything else depends on. Read the Start sector of the Linux partition from the mmls output and write it in your notes. Every Sleuth Kit command from here on takes it as -o OFFSET.

Without the right offset, the tools read the partition table region as if it were a filesystem. They do not error helpfully — they return nothing, or nonsense. Nearly every “this command doesn't work” question in this course traces back to a missing -o.

Use your mmls output. Do not copy an offset from a classmate.

Examine the filesystem. Replace OFFSET throughout:

fsstat -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd | tee output/fsstat.txt

Record

  • Image size and type.
  • Partition scheme and the start sector you will use.
  • Filesystem type, block size, and inode count.
  • Whether this filesystem records a file creation (birth) time. Check what istat shows later and note what is missing.

Part 4 — Survey the Filesystem

Produce the full recursive listing:

fls -r -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd > output/file_listing.txt
wc -l output/file_listing.txt

Get oriented before you start searching. What top-level areas exist?

fls -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd

Then look at what is mounted and who has a home directory:

grep -E "home/|mnt/" output/file_listing.txt | grep "d/d"

Orientation questions

  1. How many entries are in the listing?
  2. How many user home directories are present, and whose?
  3. Which directory trees are clearly not part of the workstation's own operating system?
  4. Which of these areas did you already examine in Lab 2, and which are new?

Field note: more than one person used this environment legitimately. At least one account in this image handled financial data every single day as part of their job and did nothing wrong. Knowing what authorized access looks like is how you will later prove that some other access was not. Identify that account early and keep it in view.

Part 5 — Build the Filesystem Timeline

Generate a bodyfile — a machine-readable dump of every file's metadata, including deleted entries: 

fls -r -m / -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd > timeline/bodyfile.txt

Render it as a chronological timeline:

mactime -b timeline/bodyfile.txt -d > timeline/full_timeline.csv

The full timeline is large. Narrow it to the period of interest: 

mactime -b timeline/bodyfile.txt -d 2026-08-20..2026-08-21 > timeline/incident_day.csv

And to the months leading up to it:

mactime -b timeline/bodyfile.txt -d 2026-06-01..2026-08-25 > timeline/campaign_window.csv

Read the incident day:

less timeline/incident_day.csv

What you are looking for

Not suspicious filenames. Relationships. A timeline is useful because it puts unrelated subsystems on one axis: 

a file is created
      ↓  (minutes later)
a command runs
      ↓  (seconds later)
a network connection opens
      ↓  (minutes later)
the file is deleted

Any one of those events is unremarkable. The sequence is the finding. In your notes, mark every cluster of activity on 2026-08-20 where three or more unrelated things happen inside the same few minutes.

Part 6 — Timestamps Can Lie (And Which Ones Can't)

Before you build an argument on timestamps, you need to know how far they can be trusted.

Filesystem timestamps and their reliability
Timestamp Meaning Can a normal user set it directly?
Modified (mtime) File contents last changed Yes — touch -d sets it to any value
Accessed (atime) File last read Yes — and it is also unreliable because many systems do not update it on every read
Changed (ctime) Inode metadata last changed No — the kernel sets it, including when someone forges mtime
Deleted (dtime) When the inode was freed No — present on deleted inodes only

Why ctime is the one that catches people: if someone back-dates a file with touch -d, mtime obeys them — but the act of changing mtime is itself a metadata change, so ctime updates to now. The result is a file whose contents were supposedly last modified long before its own metadata was last touched. On an untampered file that ordering is essentially impossible.

Find it in this image

At least one file in this image has been timestomped. Its mtime places it well before events it clearly knows about. Find it.

Compare the timestamps on any candidate:

istat -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd <INODE>

Required analysis

  1. Which file has internally inconsistent timestamps?
  2. What does its mtime claim, and why is that claim impossible?
  3. Which timestamp exposes the inconsistency?
  4. Does timestomping prove intent to deceive? Argue both sides, then state which position the evidence actually supports.
  5. Integrity note: the ctime and deletion times (dtime) across this entire image reflect when the evidence image was built, not when the scenario happened. This filesystem also records no creation time at all. Explain, in your report, why both are limitations you must disclose rather than hide.

Part 7 — User Activity and the History That Survived

Locate the shell history files:

fls -r -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd | grep -i "bash_history"

Read that output carefully before you move on. Count the results. If you extract only the file you expected to find, you will miss the single most informative user artifact in this image.

Extract each one by inode:

icat -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd <INODE> > output/alex_bash_history.txt

Search across everything you extracted:

grep -nEi "rsync|scp|tar|curl|wget|shred|crontab|history -c" output/alex_bash_history*.txt

Analysis questions

  1. What are the last commands in the live history file, and what is notably absent from the end of it?
  2. What commands appear in the other history file that do not appear in the live one?
  3. Why did those commands survive?
  4. What does this tell you about the completeness of any single artifact?
  5. Identify every command that moved data off this machine. Record the source path, the destination, and the exact flags used.
  6. One rsync invocation uses a flag that destroys the source after a successful transfer. Which flag, and what are its forensic consequences?

Also extract and review:

  • Alex's browser history
  • Alex's SSH client configuration
  • Alex's SSH known_hosts
  • The other users' history files, for comparison

Field note: browser history is not only a record of sites visited. Search queries are statements of intent, and they are time-stamped. Read them in order.

Part 8 — Authentication Activity

Extract the authentication log:

fls -r -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd | grep "auth.log"
icat -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd <INODE> > output/auth.log
wc -l output/auth.log

Establish the baseline before you hunt for anomalies:

grep -c "Accepted" output/auth.log
grep -c "Failed" output/auth.log
grep "Failed" output/auth.log | awk '{print $NF}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

Then isolate the incident day:

grep "^Aug 20" output/auth.log

Analysis questions

  1. Confirm the Lab 2 finding: which source address produced failed authentication attempts, and at what times?
  2. Which accounts were targeted by those attempts?
  3. Which sessions succeeded on 2026-08-20, and for which accounts?
  4. What privileged commands were executed through sudo that afternoon? List them in order with their timestamps.
  5. At least one sudo entry names a destination host you have not seen in Labs 1 or 2. What is it?
  6. How does the 2026-08-20 activity compare in volume and character to a routine day in this log?

Part 9 — The Finance Application: Reading an API Access Log

The workstation holds access logs for an internal finance reporting service. This is the richest log in the image and the one that establishes what was taken.

Find and extract everything under the finance API log directory:

fls -r -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd | grep -i "finance_api"
icat -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd <INODE> > output/finance_api_access.log
icat -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd <INODE> > output/finance_api_error.log

Profile the users

These logs start with # comment lines describing the field layout. Read those first — then filter them out of every count, or they will show up as phantom users.

Who uses this API, and how much?

grep -v '^#' output/finance_api_access.log | awk 'NF {print $3}' \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

What client software does each one use?

grep -o 'agent="[^"]*"' output/finance_api_access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

Which endpoints were requested, and how often?

grep -o '"GET [^ ?"]*' output/finance_api_access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

What response codes did each user receive? Note that you cannot count fields from the end of the line here, because the user-agent string contains spaces. Match the structure of the line instead: 

sed -nE 's/^[0-9.]+ - ([^ ]+) \[[^]]*\] "[^"]*" ([0-9]+) .*/\1 \2/p' \
  output/finance_api_access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

Then pair each user with the endpoints they were refused, and the ones they were eventually granted: 

sed -nE 's/^[0-9.]+ - ([^ ]+) \[[^]]*\] "[A-Z]+ ([^ ?"]*)[^"]*" ([0-9]+) .*/\1 \3 \2/p' \
  output/finance_api_access.log | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn

Field note — the shape of an attack: a long run of 403 responses followed by 200 responses to the same endpoints is one of the most legible patterns in log analysis. It means someone tried, was refused, changed something, and then was not refused. Your job is to determine what changed.

Analysis questions

  1. Which three identities appear in this log, and what is the normal access pattern for each?
  2. Which identity's requests come from a scripted HTTP client rather than a browser? What is the client string?
  3. For the subject of your investigation: on what date do the 403 responses stop and 200 responses begin for the restricted endpoints?
  4. The error log explains how the restriction was bypassed. What exactly happened, and which configuration file on this workstation made it possible?
  5. How was that file protected? Should it have been? Check its permissions with istat.
  6. Which specific endpoints were used to pull bulk data? Note any endpoint whose behavior differs from what its parameters suggest.
  7. Sum the response sizes for the subject's successful requests. Roughly how many bytes left the application through this channel?
  8. One request on the incident day attempts to modify audit data. What was it, and did it succeed?

Important: one of these log files has a shorter date range than you might expect. Note where its coverage starts. The missing period is not missing by accident, and Part 11 is where you get it back.

Part 10 — The Finance Share

A classified file share was mounted on this workstation. Survey it: 

grep "finance_share" output/file_listing.txt | wc -l
grep "finance_share" output/file_listing.txt | head -40

Read the share's own classification notice and access log.

Analysis questions

  1. What is the data classification of this share?
  2. What does its policy say about copying contents locally?
  3. How many files does it contain, and of what types?
  4. According to the share access log and the file audit log, how did the subject's access pattern differ from the finance analyst's — in timing, in volume, and in what was read?
  5. A single bulk-read event on the incident day covers a large number of files at once. When, how many files, and how many bytes?

Part 11 — Deleted Evidence: Discovery

List everything that has been deleted:

fls -r -d -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd | tee output/deleted_files.txt
wc -l output/deleted_files.txt

There are more deleted files here than in Lab 2, and they are in more than one place. Do not stop at the first directory that looks interesting. Work through the whole list and group the results by location before you extract anything.

Note that one of the deleted paths is itself a directory that no longer exists. Its name should tell you something about intent.

Not every line is a deleted file. You will also see two entries whose name is just ^, with inode 2049 and a size of zero, under two of the large directories. Those are leftovers in directory-block slack space, not files anyone deleted. Work out how you would prove that with istat, and keep them out of your inventory.

Build an inventory before extracting:

Deleted evidence inventory (complete one row per deleted file)
# Path Inode Size Recovered? Why it matters
1          
2          
3          
…          

Inspect the metadata of each deleted inode before recovering it:

istat -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd <INODE>

Confirm the inode still reports a non-zero size and lists data blocks. If it does, the content is recoverable.

Part 12 — Recovering Text Evidence

Recover each deleted text artifact by inode:

icat -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd <INODE> > recovered/transfer_manifest.txt
sha256sum recovered/transfer_manifest.txt | tee -a hashes/recovered_hashes.txt
cat recovered/transfer_manifest.txt

Repeat for every deleted text and CSV file, hashing each one.

Hash every recovered file immediately. A recovered artifact with no hash is an assertion. A recovered artifact with a recorded hash and a recorded inode is evidence.

If recovery returns nothing

If icat produces an empty file, the inode's block pointers were cleared on deletion. Fall back to carving unallocated space: 

blkls -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd > recovered/unallocated.raw
ls -lh recovered/unallocated.raw
strings -a recovered/unallocated.raw | grep -nEi "GRAND TOTAL|tobor|Bearer|chat export"
foremost -t all -i recovered/unallocated.raw -o recovered/carved

If you use the carving path, say so in your report and explain the key difference: a file recovered by inode has a known original path, name, and set of timestamps; a carved file has only its contents. That distinction matters to how much weight your finding carries.

Part 13 — Recovering Binary Evidence (Where grep Fails)

Recover the deleted spreadsheet and archive files the same way:

icat -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd <INODE> > recovered/Q1_2026_Bank_Reconciliation.xlsx
icat -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd <INODE> > recovered/finance_packet_2026-08-20.tar.gz

Verify what you actually recovered — never trust an extension:

file recovered/*

Now try to search one the way you have searched everything so far:

grep -a "GRAND TOTAL" recovered/Q1_2026_Bank_Reconciliation.xlsx
strings recovered/Q1_2026_Bank_Reconciliation.xlsx | head

That found nothing useful, and that is the lesson. An .xlsx file is a ZIP archive of compressed XML. The text you are looking for exists, but it is DEFLATE-compressed, so no byte sequence in the file matches the words you searched for.

Any investigator who concludes “there is nothing in this file” because grep was quiet has missed the evidence entirely. Decompress first, then search.

Open the workbook

Confirm the internal structure:

unzip -l recovered/Q1_2026_Bank_Reconciliation.xlsx

Extract the worksheet and search that:

mkdir -p findings/Q1_unpacked
unzip -o recovered/Q1_2026_Bank_Reconciliation.xlsx -d findings/Q1_unpacked
grep -o "GRAND TOTAL" findings/Q1_unpacked/xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml

Or open it in a spreadsheet application:

libreoffice --calc recovered/Q1_2026_Bank_Reconciliation.xlsx

Open the archive

tar -tzvf recovered/finance_packet_2026-08-20.tar.gz
mkdir -p findings/packet
tar -xzf recovered/finance_packet_2026-08-20.tar.gz -C findings/packet
ls -lh findings/packet

Analysis questions

  1. What does file report for each recovered artifact?
  2. Why does grep fail on these and succeed on the text files?
  3. What are the internal parts of the .xlsx package?
  4. What does the archive contain, and how does its contents compare to the deleted staging directory listing from Part 11?
  5. The archive and the loose files overlap. What does packaging the same data a second time suggest about the operator's intent?

Part 14 — Follow the Money

“A lot of financial data was taken” is not a finding. A number is a finding. Quantify the exposure.

Inspect the structure of a recovered workbook:

head -c 2000 findings/Q1_unpacked/xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml

Parse it properly. This script uses only the Python standard library:

python3 - <<'PY'
import zipfile
import xml.etree.ElementTree as ET

NS = "{http://schemas.openxmlformats.org/spreadsheetml/2006/main}"
PATH = "recovered/Q1_2026_Bank_Reconciliation.xlsx"
AMOUNT_COLUMN = "I"   # confirm this against the header row first

with zipfile.ZipFile(PATH) as book:
    sheet = ET.fromstring(book.read("xl/worksheets/sheet1.xml"))

rows = sheet.findall(f"{NS}sheetData/{NS}row")
print(f"rows in sheet (including header and total): {len(rows)}")

total = 0.0
counted = 0

for row in rows[1:-1]:                       # skip header and GRAND TOTAL
    for cell in row.findall(f"{NS}c"):
        if cell.get("r", "").startswith(AMOUNT_COLUMN):
            total += float(cell.find(f"{NS}v").text)
            counted += 1

print(f"data rows summed : {counted}")
print(f"sum of amounts   : ${total:,.2f}")
PY

Count the distinct client accounts exposed in a recovered CSV:

cut -d, -f3 recovered/Client_Bank_Accounts_Master.csv | tail -n +2 | sort -u | wc -l

Cross-check your arithmetic against the recovered transfer manifest.

Complete this table in your report

Quantified data exposure
Recovered file Inode Data rows Record value (USD) Sensitive fields present
         
         
         
TOTAL —      

Analysis questions

  1. How many transaction rows, in total, were staged for transfer?
  2. What is the total record value represented by those rows?
  3. How many distinct client accounts appear?
  4. What categories of sensitive data are present? Name the specific columns.
  5. Does the figure you calculated from the recovered files agree with the figure in the recovered manifest? If not, which do you trust, and why?
  6. Precision matters here: the record value of these transactions is not the same thing as financial loss to the company. Explain the difference in one or two sentences, the way you would to a non-technical executive.

Part 15 — Messaging Application Artifacts

Desktop messaging clients leave material on disk: exported conversations, local caches, and application logs. Find them: 

grep -Ei "whatsapp|telegram|signal" output/file_listing.txt

Note that some of these appear in the deleted listing from Part 11.

Recover and review each one:

icat -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd <INODE> > recovered/chat_export.txt
sha256sum recovered/chat_export.txt | tee -a hashes/recovered_hashes.txt

Most of the conversations on this machine are completely ordinary. Family, a recreational sports league, a dentist appointment. You still have to read enough of each to rule it out, and your report should state that you did. Declaring something irrelevant without examining it is not a finding, it is an assumption.

Analysis questions

  1. How many conversation exports exist? How many are deleted?
  2. Which conversations are irrelevant to the investigation, and how did you establish that?
  3. For the relevant conversation: build a chronology of it. What is discussed, and on what dates?
  4. The conversation references a method of access, a destination, and a reason for choosing that destination. Quote each one and match it to a technical artifact elsewhere in the image that independently corroborates it.
  5. One message explains the origin of a particular name. What is the name, and what does it refer to?
  6. A second messaging client holds notes that read like operational reconnaissance. What specific system details were recorded there?
  7. The final messages describe a cleanup list. Compare it item by item against what was actually deleted. Did the operator complete the list?
  8. Identity: can you establish who the other party actually is? Be careful and be honest. State precisely what the evidence does and does not support.

Part 16 — Where Did the Data Go?

You have established what was collected. Now establish where it went, and prove it with more than one source.

Extract and examine the network and remote-access logs:

grep -E "network_connections|remote_access|vpn" output/file_listing.txt

Find the outbound transfers in the network log. Port 873 is rsync: 

grep -E " 873 | 22 " output/network_connections.log | grep "2026-08-20"

Then total the bytes recorded by the remote-access log:

grep -oE "bytes=[0-9]+" output/remote_access.log | cut -d= -f2 \
  | paste -sd+ - | bc

Compare that figure against the transfer tool's own run log, which you will find under the user's profile directory rather than in /var/log. Two logs written by two different programs are two independent sources; agreeing figures are a corroborated finding, and disagreeing figures are a finding too.

Analysis questions

  1. What is the destination hostname, and what IP address does it resolve to on this workstation? Name the file that establishes the mapping.
  2. Is that host present in the organization's asset inventory? What does the inventory file tell you?
  3. How many transfer runs occurred on the incident day? At what times, and how many bytes each?
  4. Total the incident-day transfer volume from two independent sources. Do they agree? Show both figures.
  5. How far back does the transfer activity go? This did not start on the incident day.
  6. What scheduled mechanism was running these transfers, which log proves it existed, and why can you not simply read the schedule itself?
  7. The DLP system generated alerts about this activity. How many, over what period, and what was done about them?

Field note: the DLP finding is as much about the organization as about the subject. The control fired correctly and repeatedly for two months. Nobody read it. That belongs in your recommendations, and it is the kind of observation that makes a report useful rather than merely accurate.

Part 17 — The Attribution Challenge

This is the part of the lab that closes Lab 2. Read it twice before you start.

You currently have two network facts that look unrelated:

  • From Lab 2: failed SSH authentication attempts against this workstation from 10.10.20.55, an unidentified host.
  • From Part 16: a large outbound transfer to a different address entirely.

Two addresses, apparently two machines, no connection between them. Test that assumption.

Your task

Determine whether 10.10.20.55 and the exfiltration destination are the same physical device. Then determine whose device it is.

You are not being told which files to use. That is the exercise. But here is how to think about it:

  • An IP address is a lease, not an identity. Leases are assigned, expire, and get reassigned — and something on a network records that.
  • Hardware addresses do not change when IP addresses do.
  • SSH clients remember the cryptographic identity of every host they connect to, indexed by address. If one machine is reachable at two addresses, that file will say so.
  • A host that is not in DNS has to be resolvable some other way for a hostname to work in a script.

Useful starting point:

grep -rn "10.10.20.55" output/ recovered/
grep -rn "10.10.20.55" output/file_listing.txt

Required deliverable

Produce an attribution argument supported by at least three independent artifacts. Fill in this table:

Attribution evidence
Artifact (file and inode) What it shows What it rules out
     
     
     

Then answer

  1. Are the two addresses the same device? State your confidence level and justify it.
  2. What hardware identifier ties them together, and exactly when did the address change?
  3. Why does the timing of that change matter to the Lab 2 finding?
  4. Whose device is it? What evidence connects it to a person, and what is the weakest link in that chain?
  5. Does attributing the device to a person prove that person was at the keyboard? Answer carefully.
  6. Re-read your Lab 2 conclusion about 10.10.20.55. Does it still stand? Write the corrected version.

Part 18 — Anti-Forensics

Someone attempted to remove evidence from this system. Catalogue what they did.

Look for deliberate destruction across several artifact types:

grep -nEi "shred|rm -rf|history -c|crontab -r|unset HISTFILE" output/alex_bash_history*.txt
grep -nEi "removed by external process|DELETE" output/syslog output/cron.log

Build the cleanup chronology

Anti-forensic actions
Time Action Target Succeeded? How you know
         
         
         
         

Analysis questions

  1. List every destruction action in chronological order.
  2. Which of them actually worked, and which left the data recoverable anyway?
  3. One command was intended to securely wipe a file so it could not be recovered. Was the file recovered anyway? What does that tell you about the difference between what a command promises and what the filesystem does?
  4. A rotated log file was deleted. Why was that specific file worth destroying? What did it contain that the surviving log does not?
  5. A scheduled job was removed. How do you know it ever existed?
  6. The cleanup happened within a few minutes. What does that tell you about whether it was planned or improvised? What evidence supports your answer rather than your intuition?

Part 19 — Rule Out the Alternatives

A competent investigator does not build a case. A competent investigator tries to break their own theory and reports what survives.

Test each alternative explanation against the evidence:

Alternative explanations
Alternative explanation Supported, weakened, or eliminated? Evidence
The data left via the USB drive that was attached that day    
Accessing financial reports was part of the subject's job    
The transfers were a legitimate personal backup, as a document on the system claims    
An external attacker compromised the account and acted as the user    
The service account, not the user, performed the extraction    

Two of these deserve particular care.

The USB drive is real and it was attached on the incident day. Before you cite it as the exfiltration channel, find out how many bytes were actually written to it and compare that to the network figures. The difference is several orders of magnitude.

The cover-story document on the system is also real. Check when it was written relative to the activity it describes. A document created after the fact explaining earlier behavior is itself worth noting — but say so carefully, because people do also write legitimate notes late.

Part 20 — Correlate the Evidence

You now hold findings from a dozen independent sources. Correlation is what turns them into a case.

Every major conclusion needs at least two independent supporting artifacts. Independent means a different subsystem wrote it — a shell history and a network log are independent; two lines of the same shell history are not.

Case status board
Finding Evidence #1 Evidence #2 Evidence #3 Confidence
Restricted financial endpoints were accessed without entitlement        
A service credential was reused by a human user        
Financial records were staged in a hidden local directory        
Data was transferred to a host outside the asset inventory        
That host is the same device as the Lab 2 brute-force source        
The transfers were coordinated with an outside party        
Evidence was deliberately destroyed afterwards        
The identity of the outside party is established        

Confidence levels

  • Confirmed — direct evidence from multiple independent sources.
  • Probable — strong circumstantial evidence, no contradicting evidence.
  • Possible — evidence is consistent with the claim but equally consistent with other explanations.
  • Unsupported — insufficient evidence to make the claim at all.

At least one row above should end up marked “Unsupported.” If every row in your table reads “Confirmed,” you have stopped investigating and started advocating. Full marks are available for correctly identifying what you cannot prove.

Part 21 — Build the Incident Timeline

Create your reconstruction:

nano timeline/incident_timeline.md

Your timeline must contain at least 15 significant events and must span the entire campaign, not just the incident day. The earliest relevant event in this case is months before 2026-08-20.

Incident timeline template
Date / Time Event Evidence source (file + inode) Actor Phase Confidence
           
           
           
           

Use these phase labels

  1. Preparation — tooling, access, infrastructure put in place
  2. Reconnaissance — probing for what is reachable
  3. Privilege / credential abuse — obtaining access not granted
  4. Collection — gathering and staging data
  5. Exfiltration — moving data out
  6. Anti-forensics — destroying evidence
  7. Detection — when and how the organization noticed

Do not assume every phase occurred, and do not force an event into a phase to make the narrative tidier. If a phase is absent from the evidence, say so.

Part 22 — What You Cannot Determine

Create:

nano notes/limitations.md

For each question below, answer Yes, No, or Cannot Determine, and explain why in one or two sentences.

  1. Can you prove which human being was physically at the keyboard?
  2. Can you prove the data arrived intact at the destination host?
  3. Can you prove the data was opened, read, or used after it arrived?
  4. Can you identify the external party in the messaging conversation?
  5. Can you prove money changed hands?
  6. Can you prove the subject acted alone?
  7. Can you establish the exact total of data exfiltrated across the whole campaign, not just the incident day?
  8. Can you prove a particular file was ever opened, as opposed to merely copied?
  9. Can you rely on this image's ctime and deletion times? Why or why not?
  10. Can you prove the subject's stated intent?

What you would request next. List the evidence you would ask for if this were a real matter — the destination device, network capture, mail and messaging provider records, physical access logs, HR records, the finance application's server-side audit database. For each, state the specific question it would answer. Vague requests for “more logs” score nothing.

Part 23 — The Forensic Report

Produce:

report/forensic_report.pdf

Write it for two audiences at once: a general counsel who needs the first page to be decisive and plain, and an opposing expert who will check every claim in the appendices.

Required sections

  1. Executive Summary — one page maximum. What happened, what was taken, how much, where it went, and what you could not establish. No tool names, no inode numbers, no jargon.
  2. Scope and Authority — what was examined, what was not, and what questions the examination set out to answer.
  3. Methodology — tools and versions, and the order in which you applied them. Someone else must be able to repeat your work and get your results.
  4. Evidence Integrity — hashes, verification times, working-copy handling, and any integrity caveats including the image's build-date timestamp limitation.
  5. Evidence Examined — the full artifact table with paths, inodes, and hashes.
  6. Findings — each with supporting evidence, timestamps, interpretation, and confidence level.
  7. Quantified Data Exposure — the table from Part 14, with your methodology for arriving at the figures.
  8. Attribution Analysis — the Part 17 argument in full, including the weakest link.
  9. Incident Timeline — at least 15 events, phased.
  10. Incident Reconstruction — the chronological narrative, each claim tied to evidence.
  11. Alternative Explanations Considered — the Part 19 table and what survived it.
  12. Anti-Forensic Activity — what was destroyed, what survived, and why.
  13. Limitations — what cannot be determined from this evidence.
  14. Conclusion — direct answers to the questions in the case briefing.
  15. Recommendations — tied to findings only.
  16. Appendices — command output, screenshots with written descriptions, recovered file hashes.

Writing standard

Separate observation from interpretation, every time.

Weak: “Alex stole the financial data and sold it.”

Strong: “Recovered file X (inode N, SHA-256 …) contains 4,812 transaction records. The network connection log records a transfer of N bytes from 10.10.20.10 to the destination host at 15:03:58 on 2026-08-20, and the transfer tool's own log records the same volume at the same time. Taken together these support the conclusion that the recovered records were transferred to that host. The evidence does not establish what was done with them afterwards, or whether any payment occurred.”

The second version is longer. It is also the one that survives cross-examination.

Part 24 — Required Screenshots

Include at minimum:

  1. Evidence hash verification
  2. mmls partition analysis showing your offset
  3. fsstat filesystem details
  4. mactime timeline output for the incident day
  5. istat showing the timestamp inconsistency from Part 6
  6. The deleted-file listing from fls -r -d
  7. A recovered spreadsheet open, showing real financial rows
  8. The API log analysis showing the 403-to-200 transition
  9. The messaging artifact
  10. The attribution evidence
  11. Transfer volume totals
  12. Your completed case status board

Accessibility requirement

A screenshot is never the explanation. Every image must be accompanied by written text stating what command produced it, what the reader should notice, what it proves, and why it matters.

Your report must be fully understandable with every image removed. A reader using a screen reader, a printed black-and-white copy, or a court exhibit list must get the same information you did.

Reports that rely on screenshots to carry findings will lose points under both the documentation and the findings criteria.

Part 25 — Investigation Questions

Answer all of these in your report, with specific evidence.

Scope and sequence

  1. What is the earliest event you can tie to this activity, and what artifact establishes it?
  2. What is the last action taken on the system before acquisition?
  3. How long did the activity continue before it was detected?
  4. What triggered detection, and how does that compare to when it could have been detected?

Access and credentials

  1. What entitlement did the subject legitimately hold?
  2. How was that entitlement exceeded?
  3. Which credential was abused, who did it belong to, and when was it last rotated?
  4. Which configuration weakness made the abuse possible?

Data

  1. What specific categories of data were collected?
  2. How many transaction records, and what total record value?
  3. How many distinct client accounts were exposed?
  4. Which recovered artifact gives the most direct evidence of intent to transfer?

Exfiltration and attribution

  1. What was the exfiltration channel, and what was explicitly not the channel?
  2. What is the destination host, and is it a managed asset?
  3. How much data left on the incident day, corroborated by two sources?
  4. Are the Lab 2 brute-force source and the exfiltration destination the same device? Prove it.
  5. What is the single strongest piece of evidence in this investigation?
  6. What is the weakest or most ambiguous, and how did you handle it?

Judgement

  1. Can you prove data exfiltration occurred? State your confidence level and defend it.
  2. Can you prove who was at the keyboard?
  3. Can you determine motive from this evidence?
  4. Which of your Lab 1 or Lab 2 conclusions does this evidence change? Write the corrected version. If none changed, justify that.
  5. What is your single most important recommendation to the organization, and which specific finding supports it?

Grading Rubric — 100 Points

Lab 3 grading rubric
Category Points What earns full marks
Evidence Integrity & Working Copy 6 Both hashes verified and recorded; original untouched.
Disk & Filesystem Mapping 6 Correct offset derived and used consistently; filesystem characterized.
Filesystem Timeline 8 Bodyfile and filtered mactime output; clusters identified, not just generated.
Deleted-File Discovery & Recovery 12 All deleted files found across all locations, recovered, hashed, inodes recorded.
Financial Data Analysis & Quantified Exposure 10 Binary formats opened correctly; rows, dollars, and accounts quantified with stated method.
API / Endpoint Log Analysis 8 Three access patterns distinguished; bypass mechanism identified and explained.
Messaging Artifact Analysis 6 Relevant thread recovered and correlated; irrelevant threads examined and excluded on the record.
Exfiltration Channel & Attribution 12 Destination identified; volume corroborated by two sources; device attribution built from three independent artifacts.
Anti-Forensics & Timestamp Reliability 6 Cleanup chronology complete; timestomped file found; mtime/ctime reasoning correct.
Evidence Correlation & Alternatives 10 Status board completed with independent sources; alternatives genuinely tested, including the USB channel.
Incident Timeline 6 15+ events spanning the full campaign, each sourced and phased.
Limitations & Professional Judgement 5 Honest about what cannot be proven; specific, justified evidence requests.
Report Quality, Documentation & Accessibility 5 Observation separated from interpretation; report complete without images.
Total 100  

How to lose points fastest: stating conclusions as fact without evidence; citing one artifact where two were required; reporting “a lot of data” instead of a number; declaring an artifact irrelevant without examining it; screenshots with no written explanation; and concluding that the USB drive was the exfiltration channel.

Optional Stretch Challenges

No points. Attempt these only after the graded work is finished.

Challenge 1 — Carve it the hard way

Recover one deleted spreadsheet without using its inode. Extract unallocated space with blkls, carve with foremost, and compare the SHA-256 of the carved file against your inode-recovered copy. 

blkls -o OFFSET working/CYBR2800_Lab3_Working.dd > recovered/unallocated.raw
foremost -t all -i recovered/unallocated.raw -o recovered/carved
sha256sum recovered/carved/*/*.zip recovered/Q1_2026_Bank_Reconciliation.xlsx

Do the hashes match? If not, why not? Which method would you rely on in court, and what does the other one still give you?

Challenge 2 — Build the detection rule

Write a detection rule, in plain language or pseudocode, that would have caught this activity in June rather than in August. It must:

  • Fire on the actual behavior present in the logs.
  • Not fire on the legitimate finance analyst's daily work.
  • Not fire on the scheduled service account's nightly job.

State which log sources it consumes and estimate its false-positive rate against the data in this image. Writing a rule that catches everything is easy; writing one the organization would actually leave enabled is the challenge.

Investigator's Challenge

Imagine presenting these findings to someone who has never taken a cybersecurity course — a juror, a board member, a reporter.

You may not say:

“The log says this, so that's what happened.”

Say something closer to:

“The application recorded which reports were requested and how large each response was. Separately, the network equipment recorded data leaving the building. Separately again, a file we recovered after it had been deleted lists exactly those reports and totals them. Three systems that do not talk to each other recorded the same event within the same few minutes. That is why we are confident, and here is the one part we still cannot establish.”

That is the difference between finding artifacts and conducting an investigation, and it is what this three-lab sequence has been building toward.

Final Investigator Questions

Answer both at the end of your report.

1. If this were a real matter rather than a classroom exercise, what additional evidence would you collect before making a final determination — and what specific question would each item answer?

2. In Lab 2 you concluded that the activity could not be shown to be malicious from the evidence then available. That was correct at the time. Describe what changed, and explain why withholding judgement in Lab 2 was good practice rather than a failure to reach a conclusion.

The goal was never to prove a theory. The goal is to determine what the evidence can actually support, and to say so plainly — including the parts that do not fit.

Accessibility & Student Support

This assignment is designed to support different learning needs. Written explanations are required in addition to screenshots so that the investigation can be understood without relying on visual information. All required findings can be reached using command-line tools and text output alone.

If you encounter an accessibility barrier, a technical problem, or difficulty with the forensic concepts, contact your instructor before the submission deadline. If a specific tool is not accessible to you, ask — in most cases there is an equivalent command-line path to the same evidence.
